title: Working with Files & JSON
subtitle: Read and write text and JSON files safely using pathlib, context managers (with), and explicit UTF-8 encoding.

sections.heading: Context managers and pathlib
paragraphs: Always open files using a with block (a context manager) so Python automatically closes the file handle even if an error happens halfway through reading or writing.

Modern Python also provides pathlib.Path for clean, cross-platform paths and concise helpers like path.write_text(..., encoding="utf-8") and path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"). (In this browser notebook, files are stored in Pyodide's virtual in-memory filesystem.)

sections.heading: Serializing structured data with json
paragraphs: The standard library json module converts Python dictionaries and lists to JSON strings (json.dumps) or writes them straight to a file (json.dump), and parses them back with json.loads / json.load.
bullets: Always specify encoding="utf-8" when reading or writing text files.
JSON supports dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and null (None)—not Python set or custom objects directly.

marginNote.title: Common Mistakes: json.dumps vs. json.dump
paragraphs: json.dumps(obj) (with an s) returns a string; json.dump(obj, file) writes directly into an open file object.
Passing a file handle to json.dumps or forgetting the file handle in json.dump is a classic beginner TypeError.

mainCell.title: Saving and loading structured records with pathlib and json
mainCell.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path

settings_path = Path("app_config.json")
config = {
    "app": "PyFolio",
    "theme": "dark",
    "recent_lessons": [1, 2, 3],
}

# Write formatted JSON safely
with settings_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(config, f, indent=2)

# Read it back and verify round-trip
with settings_path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print("File exists in virtual FS:", settings_path.exists())
print("Loaded JSON:\n" + json.dumps(loaded, indent=2))

breakIt.title: Try Breaking It: Fix the json.dumps vs json.dump confusion & non-serializable set
breakIt.prompt: This snippet tries to write a Python `set` into JSON (which JSON does not support!) and mixes up `json.dump` with `json.dumps`. Convert the set to a sorted `list` and pass the file handle `f` to `json.dump`.
breakIt.buggyCode:
import json
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("tags.json")
payload = {"tags": {"python", "json", "files"}}  # Bug 1: sets are not JSON-serializable

with out.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    # Bug 2: json.dumps returns a string; it doesn't take a file handle as 2nd arg!
    json.dumps(payload, f)

print(out.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
breakIt.hint: Replace `{"python", "json", "files"}` with `sorted({"python", "json", "files"})` (a list) and call `json.dump(payload, f, indent=2)`.
breakIt.solution:
import json
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("tags.json")
payload = {"tags": sorted({"python", "json", "files"})}

with out.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(payload, f, indent=2)

print(out.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

quiz.question: Why should files be opened with `with Path(...).open(...) as f:`?
options: The context manager guarantees the file is closed automatically when the block exits, even on errors.
It encrypts the file contents automatically.
It converts text files into binary executables.
quiz.explanation: Context managers (`with`) handle setup and teardown reliably so file descriptors don't leak.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `json.load(f)` and `json.loads(s)`?
options: `json.load(f)` reads from an open file object; `json.loads(s)` parses a JSON string.
quiz.explanation: The `s` suffix in `loads` / `dumps` stands for string.

quiz.question: Which Python built-in type cannot be serialized directly to JSON without conversion?
quiz.explanation: JSON has arrays (`list`) and objects (`dict`), but no set type—convert sets to `list` or `sorted(my_set)` first.
